claim: In a Vero survey of Southeast Asian influencers, brand sponsorship contracts account for approximately 90% of influencer income, making SEA creator earnings structurally sponsorship-dominated rather than platform-ad-revenue-dominated.
stance_target: The position that US/Western creator-income findings built on platform ad revenue (YouTube AdSense), subscriptions (Patreon), and tipping do not transfer to Southeast Asia, where income composition is different in kind
scope_conditions: Indonesia, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam; survey of ~150 influencers (N disclosed only in NetInfluencer's write-up, not in the white paper); published c. late 2024 for 2025 outlook; respondents recruited from an agency's active-influencer network
quoted_support: These days, as much as 90% of influencers' income comes from brand sponsorship contracts, Vero's survey finds. Most influencers post sponsored content at least once a week, balancing brand promotions with regular engagement.
numbers: at least once a week sponsored posting

claim: 86% of brand partnerships with Southeast Asian influencers are structured on a per-project basis rather than as ongoing retainers, making income episodic by contractual design.
stance_target: The position that SEA creator income is structurally precarious and non-recurring, so monthly-income point estimates understate volatility and cannot be annualised
scope_conditions: 5 SEA countries; ~150 self-selected active influencers; c. 2024; no sampling frame or response rate disclosed
quoted_support: 29% of influencers cited long-term partnership opportunities as a major consideration for prioritizing brand collaborations. This number is higher in Thailand (32%) and reflects a desire among influencers for enduring relationships with brands, as 86% of brand partnerships are structured on a per-project basis.

claim: The only multi-country creator-side survey of Southeast Asia in this corpus reports no income distribution, no attrition rate, no channel-survival figure, and no time-to-first-income measure, and discloses no sample size within the publication itself.
stance_target: The position that Southeast Asian quantitative evidence on creator attrition and income distribution does not exist in the accessible literature, so US/Western findings cannot be checked against a regional counterpart
scope_conditions: Audited absence: full text of the Vero white paper reviewed; percentages are reported for platform use, content strategy, collaboration preferences and technology outlook only; the sample size appears nowhere in the document and had to be recovered from third-party trade press
quoted_support: Despite the challenges they face, influencers in Southeast Asia are optimistic about the future of their careers, with sustainability scores averaging 4.02/5.
numbers: sample size not stated in source

claim: Southeast Asian influencers rank lack of creative freedom as their most common challenge in sponsored collaborations, followed by unrealistic brand expectations, but these are grievances of active creators and are not documented reasons for quitting.
stance_target: The position that documented reasons creators give for quitting are available for Southeast Asia; they are not, and active-creator grievance data is the nearest available substitute
scope_conditions: 5 SEA countries; ~150 currently-active influencers, so anyone who already quit is structurally excluded from the sample; c. 2024
quoted_support: Most Southeast Asian influencers consider the lack of creative freedom a major challenge in sponsored collaborations. [...] Unrealistic expectations rank as the second most common challenge faced by influencers, particularly in Singapore and Thailand.
numbers: about a third decline off-values brand requests

claim: Platform use among Southeast Asian influencers is Instagram-led for activity (78%) with near-universal TikTok presence (81%), but TikTok is the primary platform for only 39% of Vietnamese and 26% of Thai influencers.
stance_target: The position that platform-specific attrition and income findings from single-platform Western studies (YouTube channel survival, Twitch payouts, Patreon) map onto SEA creators, who operate a different and multi-platform mix
scope_conditions: 5 SEA countries; ~150 respondents total, so country-level splits rest on cells of roughly 30 and cannot support inference; c. 2024
quoted_support: Instagram has become the go-to platform where 78% of influencers in Southeast Asia are most active. [...] 81% of Southeast Asian influencers in our survey having some form of presence on TikTok.

claim: Southeast Asian influencers reported a 72% increase in sponsored content requests within a single year, indicating demand-side expansion rather than creator-side income growth.
stance_target: The position that growth in the SEA creator economy is measured on the brand-demand side, leaving creator-side earnings and survival unmeasured
scope_conditions: 5 SEA countries; ~150 active influencers self-reporting; year not precisely dated in source ('this year', c. 2024); regional influencer segment CAGR given as 10.83%
quoted_support: With a striking 72% increase in sponsored content requests this year, as noted by surveyed influencers in Southeast Asia, we can expect an even greater surge in content sponsorships and collaborative campaigns throughout 2025.
numbers: USD 480 billion global influencer advertising market by 2027
